pthm-fd-px04-prediction:
## Statement

Let $h,a,\rho_0,\mu>0$, $p_0,G,V_0,V_1\in\mathbb R$, and $\nu=\mu/\rho_0$. Use SI units: lengths in metres, $p_0$ in pascals, velocities in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, density in $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, viscosity in $\mathrm{Pa\,s}$, pressure in pascals, and $G$ in pascals per metre. Let $e_x,e_y,e_z$ be the standard Cartesian unit vectors. In Cartesian coordinates, $\operatorname{div}u=\partial_xu_x+\partial_yu_y+\partial_zu_z$ and $(\Delta u)_i=\partial_{xx}u_i+\partial_{yy}u_i+\partial_{zz}u_i$. The stress is $\sigma=-pI+2\mu D$, with $D=(\nabla u+\nabla u^{\mathsf T})/2$ and $(\nabla u)_{ij}=\partial_{x_j}u_i$. The selected constant-density incompressible Newtonian model has
$$\partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u+\rho_0^{-1}\nabla p-\nu\Delta u=0,\qquad \operatorname{div}u=0.$$

For the infinite plane channel
$\Omega_{\rm ch}=\{(x,y,z):x,z\in\mathbb R,\ 0<y<h\}$, set
$u=(v(y),0,0)$, $p=p_0-Gx$, with $v\in C^2([0,h])$ and wall values $v(0)=V_0$, $v(h)=V_1$. The unique profile within this one-dimensional ansatz is
$$v(y)=V_0+(V_1-V_0)\frac yh+\frac{G}{2\mu}y(h-y).$$
Its volume flux per unit width in $z$, measured in $\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$, and channel shear values are
$$Q_{\rm ch}=\int_0^h v(y)\,dy=\frac h2(V_0+V_1)+\frac{Gh^3}{12\mu},\qquad \sigma_{xy}(0)=\mu\frac{V_1-V_0}{h}+\frac{Gh}{2},\quad \sigma_{xy}(h)=\mu\frac{V_1-V_0}{h}-\frac{Gh}{2}.$$

For the infinite circular pipe
$\Omega_a=\{(x,y,z):x\in\mathbb R,\ y^2+z^2<a^2\}$, take $x$ as axial coordinate, $r=(y^2+z^2)^{1/2}$, $u=(w(r),0,0)$, and $p=p_0-Gx$. Require $w(a)=0$ and require the radial field $(y,z)\mapsto w((y^2+z^2)^{1/2})$ to be $C^2$ on the closed disk. The unique profile within this ansatz is
$$w(r)=\frac{G}{4\mu}(a^2-r^2),\qquad Q_{\rm pipe}=\int_0^a2\pi r\,w(r)\,dr=\frac{\pi Ga^4}{8\mu}.$$
The pipe volume flux is in $\mathrm{m^3\,s^{-1}}$. For $r>0$ let $e_r=(0,y/r,z/r)$ and define the radial-axial stress component by $\sigma_{rx}=e_r\cdot\sigma e_x$; it is $\sigma_{rx}(r)=\mu w'(r)=-Gr/2$.

Both fields satisfy the exact stationary Navier–Stokes equations for every allowed parameter choice and also the corresponding steady Stokes equations because their time derivatives and convective accelerations vanish. Uniqueness is only within the stated ansätze; pipe uniqueness uses full-disk regularity at the axis. These infinite or fully developed geometries give no finite entrance or exit error estimate, stability or transition claim, observation, or empirical-validity claim.

def-fd-incompressible-euler-model.physical_scope: Smooth ideal inviscid incompressible continuum with stated boundary/initial data; no empirical derivation of zero viscosity.

def-fd-incompressible-euler-model:
## Definition

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open time interval measured in seconds and $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ an open spatial region measured in metres in a Newtonian Cartesian inertial chart. Let $\rho_0>0$ be constant in $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, $u\in C^2(I\times\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ velocity in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, and $p\in C^1(I\times\Omega)$ pressure in pascals. Define $(\operatorname{div}u)=\sum_{i=1}^3\partial_{x_i}u_i$ and $D_tu=\partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u$. The selected unforced incompressible Euler branch is
$$\rho=\rho_0,\qquad \operatorname{div}u=0,\qquad \rho_0D_tu+\nabla p=0.$$
Here $p$ is a constraint multiplier. No viscous stress or equation of state is included. Initial, wall, periodic and other boundary data are separate inputs. This is an adopted model formulation, not a derivation of empirical validity or an assertion of solution existence.

## Statement

Let $\rho_0>0$, vortex circulation parameter $\kappa\ne0$ in $\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$, and angular speed $\Omega\ne0$ in $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$. Define $e_r=(x/r,y/r,0)$ and $e_\theta=(-y/r,x/r,0)$. In Cartesian coordinates, $\operatorname{div}u=\partial_xu_x+\partial_yu_y+\partial_zu_z$ and $\operatorname{curl}u=(\partial_yu_z-\partial_zu_y,\partial_zu_x-\partial_xu_z,\partial_xu_y-\partial_yu_x)$. On the punctured region $r=(x^2+y^2)^{1/2}>0$, set $e_\theta=(-y/r,x/r,0)$, $u=\kappa r^{-1}e_\theta$, and $p=p_\infty-\rho_0\kappa^2/(2r^2)$. This steady field solves the selected unforced incompressible Euler model, is divergence-free and curl-free on its domain, and has circulation $2\pi\kappa$ around every positively oriented circle about the axis. A differentiable global potential means a single-valued $C^1$ function $\phi$ on the domain with $u=\nabla\phi$; none exists.

On a connected open region, the steady solid-rotation field $u=\Omega(-y,x,0)$, $p=p_0+\rho_0\Omega^2(x^2+y^2)/2$ also solves that model. A streamline here is an integral curve of the steady velocity field. Its Bernoulli function $B=|u|^2/2+p/\rho_0=p_0/\rho_0+\Omega^2r^2$ is constant along each streamline but is not one constant across streamlines at different radii. These are exact conditional model fields, not viscous-flow or empirical claims.

post-fd-creeping-force-balance.physical_scope: Ideal creeping-flow alternative, prescribed stress/data, constant density, no unconditional NS approximation error or empirical premise.

post-fd-creeping-force-balance:
## Postulate

For a smooth constant-density incompressible Newtonian continuum in an inertial Cartesian chart, select the steady zero-inertia alternative force balance on an open region $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$. Let $\rho_0>0$ be constant mass density, $\mu>0$ constant dynamic viscosity, $u\in C^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ velocity, $p\in C^1(\Omega)$ pressure and $b\in C^0(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ specified body acceleration. In SI units, $\rho_0$ is $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, $\mu$ is $\mathrm{Pa\,s}$, $u$ is $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $b$ is $\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, and $p$ is in pascals. Adopt
$$\operatorname{div}u=0,\qquad \sigma=-pI+2\mu D,\qquad \operatorname{div}\sigma+\rho_0b=0,\qquad D=\tfrac12(\nabla u+\nabla u^{\mathsf T}).$$
Here $(\nabla u)_{ij}=\partial_j u_i$ and $(\operatorname{div}\sigma)_i=\sum_j\partial_j\sigma_{ij}$. This is an alternative zero-inertia branch: the full material-acceleration momentum equation is not also imposed on the same field. For constant $\mu$, the adopted balance is equivalent to $-\nabla p+\mu\Delta u+\rho_0b=0$. The Postulate does not assert that small Reynolds number alone yields this branch, provide an approximation error or solution-existence result, or establish empirical validity. Boundary and far-field data remain separate.

def-fd-creeping-stokes-model.physical_scope: Ideal creeping-flow auxiliary model with specified data/decay/regularity; no empirical premises.

def-fd-creeping-stokes-model:
## Definition

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open, $\rho_0>0$ constant density, $\mu>0$ constant viscosity, $u\in C^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ velocity, $p\in C^1(\Omega)$ pressure, and $b\in C^0(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ specified body acceleration. Set $D=(\nabla u+\nabla u^{\mathsf T})/2$, $(\operatorname{div}\sigma)_i=\sum_j\partial_j\sigma_{ij}$ and $(\Delta u)_i=\sum_j\partial_{jj}u_i$. The selected steady creeping Stokes branch is
$$\operatorname{div}u=0,\qquad \sigma=-pI+2\mu D,\qquad \operatorname{div}\sigma+\rho_0b=0.$$
Equivalently, $-\nabla p+\mu\Delta u+\rho_0b=0$. The definition uses the zero-inertia alternative force balance and does not also impose the full material-acceleration equation on the same field. Boundary, far-field, geometry and decay conditions are separate. The force-free sphere application selects $b=0$. This is not a finite-Reynolds-number approximation theorem.

pthm-fd-px09-prediction:
## Statement

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open time interval measured in seconds, $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ nonempty and open in metres, and $P:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ be $C^2$. Use SI units: $u$ in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $\rho$ in $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, $P$ in pascals, and $V,h,B$ in $\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-2}}$. Let $\rho:I\times\Omega\to(0,\infty)$ have continuous first time and spatial derivatives, $u:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ have continuous first time, first spatial and second spatial derivatives, and $V:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ be a time-independent $C^2$ potential per unit mass. Adopt the barotropic Euler equations with conservative body acceleration $-\nabla V$:
$$\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}(\rho u)=0,\qquad \partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u=-\rho^{-1}\nabla(P(\rho))-\nabla V.$$
For a fixed $\rho_{\rm ref}>0$, define $h(q)=\int_{\rho_{\rm ref}}^qP'(r)/r\,dr$. A steady streamline is a $C^1$ curve $x:J\to\Omega$ satisfying $x'(s)=u(x(s))$. If $u,\rho$ are steady, then
$$B=\frac{|u|^2}{2}+h(\rho)+V$$
is constant along each streamline. If additionally $\operatorname{curl}u=0$ on a connected component, then $B$ is constant throughout that component; here $\operatorname{curl}$ is the Cartesian curl. For every closed $C^1$ material loop $X:J\times[0,1]\to\Omega$ with $X(t,0)=X(t,1)$, $X_t=u(t,X)$, and continuous $X_s,X_{ts}$, the circulation
$$\Gamma(t)=\int_0^1u(t,X(t,s))\cdot X_s(t,s)\,ds$$
is constant. The conservative body acceleration and local barotropic branch are model inputs; no statement concerns shocks, nonbarotropic pressure, nonconservative forcing, or viscous circulation.

In particular, take $P(\rho)=c^2\rho$ with $c>0$ in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $V=0$, angular speed $\Omega_0\ne0$ in $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, density $\rho_c,\rho_{\rm ref}>0$ in $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, angular and reference lengths $R,H$ in metres, and the open cylinder $D=\{(x,y,z):x^2+y^2<R^2,\ |z|<H\}$ for $R,H>0$ measured in metres. Set $r=(x^2+y^2)^{1/2}$, $e_\theta=(-y/r,x/r,0)$ for $r>0$, $u=\Omega_0(-y,x,0)$, and $\rho=\rho_c\exp(\Omega_0^2r^2/(2c^2))$ for $\rho_c>0$. These smooth fields satisfy both equations. For each circle of radius $\ell\in(0,R)$ at height $|z_0|<H$, the material evolution $X(t,\theta)=(\ell\cos(\theta+\Omega_0t),\ell\sin(\theta+\Omega_0t),z_0)$ has circulation $2\pi\Omega_0\ell^2$. Its Bernoulli function is
$$B=c^2\log(\rho_c/\rho_{\rm ref})+\Omega_0^2r^2.$$
It is constant along each circular streamline but varies between radii, since $\operatorname{curl}u=(0,0,2\Omega_0)\ne0$. This is a conditional prediction of the stated smooth barotropic model, not an empirical claim about viscous flow.

pthm-fd-px13-prediction:
## Statement

Let $a,\rho_0>0$, $p_\infty\in\mathbb R$, $U\in\mathbb R^3$, with lengths in metres, velocity in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, density in $\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$ and pressure in pascals, and $\Omega_a=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:r=|x|>a\}$. Define $n=x/r$, Cartesian $\operatorname{div}u=\partial_xu_x+\partial_yu_y+\partial_zu_z$, $\phi(x)=(U\cdot x)(1+a^3/(2r^3))$, $u=\nabla\phi$, and $p=p_\infty+\rho_0(|U|^2-|u|^2)/2$. In the selected unforced incompressible Euler model these smooth fields solve $(u\cdot\nabla)u+\rho_0^{-1}\nabla p=0$, div $u=0$, tend uniformly in direction to $U,p_\infty$ at infinity, and have $u\cdot n=0$ at $r=a$. On the surface the velocity is $u=\tfrac32(U-(U\cdot n)n)$, generally nonzero tangent to the sphere. Thus the boundary is impermeable with slip, not no-slip. For the inviscid stress $\sigma_E=-pI$ and sphere normal $n=x/a$ pointing from center into exterior,
$$\int_{|x|=a}\sigma_E n\,dS=-\int_{|x|=a}p n\,dS=0.$$
This is an exact inviscid mathematical-model prediction, neither zero viscous drag nor an observed force.
